titulo: robos-impressos — print your pet robot’s body at home
meta: Three robot bodies to 3D print (dinosaur, capybara, and square robot), with room for servos, motors, Arduino, and Raspberry Pi. Parts generated by code and checked by a script. Phase 1: mechanics.
hero_chip: Robots to print at home · phase 1: the body · project not yet printed
hero_h1: Your pet robot starts with your 3D printer
hero_lead: You want an animal-like robot at home. Ready-made kits are expensive, and projects found online often don't fit together: hours of printing and filament wasted. robos-impressos provides the body: three models with a place for each motor and board, checked by a program before you print. Making it move on its own (wiring and programming) is the next phase.
hero_alt: Illustration: a dinosaur, a capybara, and a toy square robot beside a 3D printer
resumo: You want to build a friendly robot at home and don’t know where to start with the body. robos-impressos is a set of three robot bodies to 3D print: a dinosaur and a capybara about 33 cm tall that roll across the floor, and a square desktop robot with a screen for a face. Each one already has the right space for the motors, servos (small motors that turn to an angle and stop), battery, and Arduino and Raspberry Pi boards. It’s for anyone with access to a 3D printer with a 256 mm build plate who wants to build, learn, or teach robotics. This is phase 1, just the body and its fittings: wiring, voice, and intelligence are for phase 2. And an honest note: this is a digital project checked by a script; no one has printed these parts yet.
grade_alt: Illustration showing six steps: choose a model, print, fit the servos, assemble the shell, turn the head, ready for phase 2
nota_ilustracao: The two banners above are AI-generated illustrations. All other images on this page are renders: computer-generated images made from the project files, not photos of an assembled robot.
modelos_sub: All three use the same servos and screws. The dinosaur and capybara share the same skeleton inside: only the shell changes.
dino_alt: Render of the assembled dinosaur: green, with big blue eyes, a cream belly, and blue spikes
dino_txt: A big-eyed baby dinosaur with blue spikes. It rolls on two wheels hidden inside its legs and rests on a ball. It turns and tilts its head, opens its mouth, and moves both arms.
capi_alt: Render of the assembled capybara: orange, with a brown snout, green bandana, and blue ring around the thigh
capi_txt: Seated, with a green bandana. The wheels sit inside the thighs, behind the blue ring, and the support ball sits inside the tail. It turns and tilts its head and opens its mouth.
cubo_alt: Render of the square robot: a cube-shaped head with a screen, on a fork and base
cubo_txt: Made for a desk; it doesn’t roll. Its head is a cube with a 3.5-inch screen that displays its eyes and mouth. It turns almost halfway around in either direction (nearly a full turn in total) and tilts up and down.
modelos_nota: The animals ended up 33 cm tall, a little above the 30 cm target: the battery, Arduino, and Raspberry Pi need to fit stacked inside. Parts list for each one:
como_h2: Inside: a skeleton with the shell on top
como_sub: The dark skeleton carries the weight. The colorful shell just covers it and comes off without taking anything apart.
esq_alt: Render showing only the dinosaur’s skeleton: chassis, wheels, motors, board trays, and neck
como1_p: One piece forms the floor, the walls where the motors are screwed in, and the neck support. The Arduino tray and Raspberry Pi tray slide between the walls like drawers. The battery sits underneath them.
exp_alt: Render of the dinosaur exploded view, with each part spaced apart
como2_p: The belly, back, legs, tail, and head are separate parts, held together by hidden screws. Except for the tail and back (5 screws), the panels slide out from the rear like drawers.
capiv_alt: Render of the capybara from four angles
como3_p: The top of the body is a sphere, and the head is a helmet that turns and tilts around it with 2 to 3 mm of clearance. That lets the head move in every direction without leaving a gap.

como4_t: The square one turns almost a full rotation
como4_p: A standard servo only turns halfway. Two printed gears double that rotation, and the cables run up inside the hollow neck tube without getting tangled.

prova_sub: A script (a small program) opens the print files, assembles the robot on the computer, and looks for problems. These are the numbers from the latest run, across all three models.
num1: parts to print, all closed and complete in the file
num2: parts intersecting one another, across all tested positions
num3: the thinnest wall measured in the shells (the target was at least 2 mm)
num4: is the largest part; the printer's build plate is 256 mm
barra_titulo: Estimated print hours per model (without a slicer: approximate only)
prova_ok_li:
• Each file is a closed solid made of a single body.
  • Every part fits on the 256 × 256 × 256 mm build plate.
  • No part occupies the space of another part or a component (servo, motor, board, battery), with the head, mouth, and arms at the extremes.
  • Every part can reach its position: the script brings them in one at a time, in assembly order, and flags any collision with what is already assembled.
  • No part is floating in the air, and the center of gravity falls inside the supports, with clearance.
  • The test itself is tested: one part is deliberately moved 3 mm, and the script must flag it.
prova_nao_t: What only printing can tell you
prova_nao_li:
• No one has printed or assembled these parts yet.
  • Print time and filament use are estimates based on volume.
  • Some component measurements have no official source (servo tabs, motor driver holes): they are marked, and you should measure your own part first.
  • The script does not test strength, whether a screwdriver can reach every screw, or the 3 mm fit of the servos in the arms and mouth.
plano_h2: From file to assembled robot body
plano_sub: Five steps, no programming needed. At the end, you have the assembled body, with servos and motors in place; making it move is phase 2.
pl1_p: The square robot is the simplest (14 parts). The dinosaur and capybara each have about 38 parts, and you can swap one shell for the other later.
pl2_p: One micro servo and a pack of M3 threaded inserts are enough for the test. The rest (servos, motors with wheels, battery holder, switch, M3 screws) are common parts at electronics stores in Brazil. The servos and motors are only for checking the fit at this stage: they won't move yet.
pl3_p: It's a 7 cm plate that tests how the servo, screws, and pins fit on your printer. Less than an hour of printing can save you from redoing a five-hour part.
pl4_p: The parts come laid out in the right orientation and separated by color. The skeleton is printed in PETG, which is more durable; the shell in PLA.
pl5_p: First the skeleton with motors and servos, then the shell, and finally the head. The order, screw by screw, is in the project plan.

tec_sub: You don't need this section to understand what you've read above.
oque_h2: Parts generated from code, not drawn by hand
oque_sub: Everything comes from a file of measurements. If you change the servo or your printer’s clearance, change one number and generate it again.
p1_p: cad/parametros.py stores clearances, measurements for each component (with the source next to it), and the shape of each robot.
p2_p: cad/verificar.py reads the exported STL files and rejects open parts, oversized parts, thin walls, parts intersecting each other, parts that cannot reach their position, and robots that tip over.
p3_p: The chassis, trays, fork, and neck cradle use the same files for the dinosaur and the capybara (pecas/comum/).
fluxo_sub: The animals’ outer shells are made by adding rounded shapes together and turning them into a mesh; holes, pockets, and cuts are exact operations applied on top.
fx1_p: Creates STL and 3MF files for each part, already oriented for printing, the complete assembly (montagem.glb), and the build plate layouts.
fx2_p: Assembles the robot from the files, moves the joints to their limits, measures overlaps by shared volume, and rebuilds the assembly one part at a time.
fx3_p: Blender produces the images on this page: assembled, exploded, skeleton, and build plates.

g1_p: The print files are ready in the pecas/ folder, in STL and 3MF formats. If you just want to print, download the ZIP, extract it, and open the files in your slicer: you don't need a terminal or Python.

If the fit is too tight or loose, adjust the clearance in cad/parametros.py, in the FOLGA block (componente for the servo, encaixe for the pin, inserto_d for the insert), then regenerate it in step 3.

g5_p: Assembly order for the dinosaur and capybara:
g5_li:
• Install the M3 threaded inserts in the parts using heat.
  • Screw the two motors to the chassis walls from the outside, with the motor facing up.
  • Attach the support ball with the cover underneath.
  • Mount the head-turning servo on top of the chassis, then the fork, the second servo, and the cradle.
  • Slide in the battery and board trays from the rear.
  • Close the torso from the front, and only then fit the wheels from the sides.
  • Belly panel, back, legs or thighs, tail.
  • Assemble the head on the bench (build plate under the skull, mouth servo, jaw, eyes), then lower the whole assembly onto the neck: two screws from above, hidden under the crest.
  • Spikes, claws, ears, and bandana are press-fit or glued in place.
g6_li:
• Servo on the base floor and Arduino beside it; then the large gear on top of the servo.
  • Insert the battery through the rear door.
  • Neck tube under the cover, then the cover on the base.
  • Fork on top of the tube, with three long screws.
  • Raspberry Pi, screen, and the second servo on the head frame.
  • Head shell from the rear, screen frame from the front.
  • Head between the fork arms and the rear door.

f2_h2: There is already a place for everything

f2_1b: Raspberry Pi in the head, Arduino in the base
f2_2b: 4 holes at the top of the head and 4 in the base lid
f2_3a: ring inside the belly panel; the panel slots form the grille
f2_3b: ring and grille at the front of the base
f2_4a: posts inside the snout (dinosaur) or forehead (capybara); moves with the head
f2_4b: posts behind the frame, above the screen

custo_nota: Estimated component cost, excluding the printer, filament, and Raspberry Pi: R$ 330 to 560 per animal and R$ 260 to 430 for the square robot (prices from Brazilian stores in November 2026; estimate).
ferramentas: Tools: soldering iron (for the inserts), small Phillips screwdriver, 2.5 mm Allen key, calipers (to measure your components), and instant glue.
pilhas_nota: Be careful with 18650 batteries: they are lithium batteries. Use a proper holder and charger, keep the terminals from touching metal, and don't charge them unattended, especially with children nearby.

pal_dl: <dt>Servo</dt><dd>A small motor that turns to an angle and stays there. It turns the head and opens the mouth.</dd><dt>Arduino and Raspberry Pi</dt><dd>Two electronic boards. The Arduino controls motors and servos; the Raspberry Pi is a small computer that handles voice and camera in phase 2.</dd><dt>Script</dt><dd>A small program. Here, it generates the parts and checks that they're correct.</dd><dt>Render</dt><dd>An image made on a computer from the 3D file. It's not a photo.</dd><dt>PLA and PETG</dt><dd>Two printing plastics. PLA gives a nice finish; PETG handles more force and heat.</dd><dt>Build plate</dt><dd>The printer's base. "12 build plates" means 12 prints, one after another.</dd><dt>M3 threaded insert</dt><dd>A threaded brass insert that is heated and pushed into the plastic so a 3 mm screw holds firmly.</dd><dt>18650 battery</dt><dd>A rechargeable lithium battery, a little larger than a standard battery.</dd><dt>Motor driver</dt><dd>A small board that lets the Arduino power the wheel motors and reverse their direction.</dd>
